excerpt: How to search for a video, use the player controls, choose a lower quality when data is short, and get back to where you stopped watching.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to watch a video on a computer or phone without losing your place. You will search for what you want, use the player, and control how much data it uses. Nothing here needs a fast connection or a new device.
A video plays in a player, which is a set of controls sitting on top of the picture. Learning five of those controls is enough to watch almost anything.
Before you start

items: A computer or phone with a browser or the video app.
A connection, even a slow one.
About fifteen minutes.

body.text: Find the video you meant to watch
Search results are ranked by many things, and the first one is not always the clearest explanation.

items: Type what you want in plain words, such as how to change a tyre.
Add a year if the topic changes often, such as phone setup 2026.
Read the title and the channel name before you click.
Look at the length. A four-minute clip beats a forty-minute one if it answers your question.
Check the upload date on anything technical, because menus move.
Open the video description, which often lists the steps in order.

body.text: You will see the results page change as you type, with suggestions appearing under the search box. Ignore the suggestions unless one of them matches your words exactly.

body.alt: A video site search results page with titles, channel names, and lengths.
body.caption: Read the title, the channel, and the length before clicking. Those three tell you most of what you need.

body.text: It looks like a long video must be more complete. Many long videos repeat themselves, and a short one often answers your question in three minutes.
The controls you will use

items: Play and pause: the triangle or two bars in the middle or at the bottom.
The timeline: the bar showing how far you have watched. Click it to jump.
Volume: the speaker icon, which also mutes.
Settings, shaped like a gear, where quality and speed live.
Full screen: the square bracket icon, or the F key on a computer.
The back arrow, which returns you to the results without losing the tab.

body.text: None of these buttons can damage anything. Pressing the wrong one changes the picture or stops it, and pressing it again puts things back.
Point at any control and a small label appears beside it naming what it does. That label is the fastest way to learn the player without a guide.

body.alt: A person watching a lesson video with the player controls visible.
body.caption: The bar at the bottom holds everything you need. The gear holds quality and speed.

body.text: When the video keeps stopping
A video that freezes while a circle spins is loading. The cause is usually the connection, not the device.

items: Open Settings in the player and choose a lower quality, such as 360p or 480p.
Pause for a minute and let the grey bar fill before you press play.
Move closer to the router, or turn off other downloads on the same connection.
Close the other tabs, which are using memory the video needs.
On a phone, switch to data if the wifi is weak, but watch your bundle.
Download the video on wifi first if the app offers it, then watch without a network.

body.text: Lower quality means a softer picture and far less data. For a lesson about a menu or a form, the softer picture is worth it.
You will see the picture soften within a few seconds, and the grey loading bar fill faster than before. The settings menu will show the current quality ticked, so you can see what you chose.
Do not worry about the picture looking rough. You are watching to learn a step, not to admire the scenery.
Coming back to where you stopped

items: Signed in, most sites remember your position and show a red bar under the video.
Signed out, write the time down, such as 6:42, and look for it when you return.
The history page lists what you watched, which is the quickest way back.
On a phone, the app keeps a resume list without any effort.
If you lose the place, drag the timeline and look for the frame you remember.
Bookmark the video if you will return to it over several days.

body.text: Saving a link is faster than searching again. Copy the address bar and keep it in a note with the reason you saved it.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a fix you can try in a minute.

items: There is no sound: the speaker icon is muted, or the wrong output is chosen.
The video will not play at all: the browser is old. Update it, or try another.
The screen is black but sound plays: the picture is playing in another window or on another screen.
The page is full of adverts: use the skip button when it appears, or the close cross on the banner.
The video is not the right one: press the browser back button and choose again.
Data disappears quickly: the quality was set high. Lower it before the next video.

body.text: Practice
One search, one pause, one quality change, and the player stops being strange.

items: Search for a short clip about a task you already know.
Pause it, jump forward, and jump back using the timeline.
Open the gear and read the quality options without changing them.
Choose a lower quality and notice the difference in the picture.
Write down the time you stopped, then find it again in history.

body.text: You can now watch a lesson video without fighting the player. In the next lesson you will read the words on screen with captions and slow a fast speaker down.

excerpt: How to turn on captions, slow down a fast speaker, speed up a slow one, and use keyboard shortcuts so a video lesson fits your pace.

body.text: This lesson teaches you three controls that make any video easier to follow: captions, pause, and speed. You will turn on subtitles, slow a fast speaker to three-quarter speed, and skip back ten seconds without touching the timeline.
A video plays at the pace of the person who made it. These controls hand that pace back to you, which matters in a noisy room or with an accent you are still learning to follow.
Before you start

items: A video open in a browser or the app.
About ten minutes.

body.text: Captions, in words on the screen

items: Look for a button marked CC in the player, usually near the volume icon.
Click it once. A small box of text appears at the bottom of the picture.
Read the first line to check the language is correct.
Open Settings, then Subtitles, if the CC button is not showing.
Choose English, or auto-generated English if that is the only option.
Click CC again to switch captions off, which gives the picture back.

body.text: You will see white text with a dark background appear over the lower part of the picture. It lags behind the voice by about a second, which is normal.

body.alt: A video playing with captions shown across the lower part of the picture.
body.caption: Captions appear over the picture. Auto-generated ones contain small errors, but the meaning is almost always clear.

body.text: It looks like captions must be typed by the person who made the video. Many are generated automatically by the platform, which is why a name or a number occasionally comes out wrong.
Slowing down a fast speaker
Nigerian English spoken quickly is fine in person and hard to follow in a recording. Speed control fixes that without asking anybody to repeat themselves.

items: Open Settings, then Playback speed.
Choose 0.75, which is three-quarter speed and still sounds natural.
Listen to one sentence and adjust if it drags.
Use 0.5 only for a hard section, such as a set of numbers.
Use 1.25 or 1.5 to move faster through a part you already know.
Set it back to Normal before you finish, so the next video starts at a normal pace.

body.text: None of this changes the video itself. The speed setting affects only your playback, and it resets when the tab closes.

body.alt: The player settings menu open showing playback speed options.
body.caption: Speed lives in the same gear menu as quality. Three-quarter speed is the most comfortable for a new accent.

body.text: Keys that save you reaching for the mouse

items: Space plays and pauses while the video has focus.
The left and right arrows skip five seconds, or ten in most players.
J and L go back and forward ten seconds on the larger sites.
The letter K pauses, and M mutes.
F fills the screen, and Escape leaves it.
The up and down arrows change the volume.

body.text: A keyboard is faster than finding a small button with a mouse, and every one of these keys works the same in the next video.
Do not worry about memorising the list. Space and the arrow keys cover most of what you need while you learn the rest.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is a setting, and none of them breaks the video.

items: The captions are in the wrong language: open Settings, then Subtitles, and choose again.
There are no captions offered: the speaker never enabled them, and no setting will invent them.
Captions cover the information: drag the caption box up or down in full screen.
The sound is deep and slow at 0.75: some players lower the pitch. Return to normal speed.
The keys do nothing: the picture is not focused. Click it once, then press them.
The video restarts when you change speed: press the left arrow to return to your place.

body.text: Practice
Try all three on one video and you will use them on every video.

items: Turn captions on and read one full sentence.
Slow the video to 0.75 and listen to a paragraph.
Press the left arrow twice and watch it skip back.
Set the speed to normal and leave full screen with Escape.
Write down which control helped you most.

body.text: You can now make a recording fit your pace instead of the other way round. In the next lesson you will use airplane mode to save battery and data when the network is not helping.

excerpt: What airplane mode turns off, when it saves battery and data, how to use it as a reset for a weak signal, and why your calls then fail.

body.text: This lesson explains airplane mode: what it switches off, when it helps, and what stops working while it is on. You will use it to save battery, to stop data charges, and to reset a network that has stopped working.
Airplane mode turns off every radio in the device: the mobile network, wifi, and Bluetooth. The phone still works as a camera, a calculator, and a place to read what you have already saved.
Before you start

items: A phone or a laptop.
About ten minutes.

body.text: Turning it on and what stops

items: Swipe down from the top of the phone screen to open the quick settings.
Tap the airplane symbol. It turns solid or coloured when it is on.
On a laptop, look for the airplane icon in the system tray or menu bar.
The signal bars disappear and a small plane appears where they were.
Calls, texts, and mobile data stop working immediately.
Wifi turns off too on most phones, though you can switch it back on by hand.

body.text: You will see the network name vanish from the top bar and the plane symbol take its place. Any app that needs the internet will show a message about no connection, which is the expected result.

body.alt: A phone quick settings panel with the airplane mode button switched on.
body.caption: The plane symbol in quick settings. Solid means on, and every radio is off until you change it.

body.text: It looks like airplane mode is only for flights. It is a general switch for cutting the radios, and people use it every day for battery and data.
Four reasons to use it on the ground

items: Battery: with no signal, the phone stops searching for a tower, which saves a great deal.
Data: nothing downloads in the background, so a small bundle lasts longer.
Weak signal: switching it on and off makes the phone look for the network again.
Charging: a phone charges faster with the radios off, especially a low-end one.
Sleep: fewer notifications at night, without hunting through settings.
A meeting or an exam: no interruptions, and you can still read saved notes.

body.text: None of this deletes anything. Messages and calls that arrive while it is on will reach you when it goes off.

body.alt: The airplane icon shown in a phone status bar.
body.caption: The small plane in the status bar tells you at a glance why nothing is loading.

body.text: The reset trick for a bad signal
When a phone shows full bars and still will not load a page, the network connection has become stuck. A quick cycle usually fixes it.

items: Turn airplane mode on and wait ten seconds.
Turn it off and watch the signal bars return.
Wait for the phone to show 4G or LTE again before opening any app.
Try the page again, which usually loads.
If it does not, restart the phone, which takes longer and fixes more.
Repeat no more than once or twice a day, since a struggling tower will not improve.

body.text: Do not worry about looking foolish for switching the network off to fix the network. Engineers do the same thing on much larger equipment.
If it goes wrong
Every case here comes from the mode staying on when you did not intend it.

items: Calls go straight to voicemail: airplane mode is still on. Check the top bar.
You cannot send a message: the phone has no network. Turn the mode off and wait.
Wifi will not connect: some phones keep wifi off after the mode. Switch wifi on by hand.
A hotspot is unavailable: tethering needs the mobile network, which is off.
The battery drains faster than before: a weak signal was the earlier cause, not the cure.
The switch is greyed out: a system setting or a device management app is blocking it.

body.text: Practice
Turn it on for ten minutes and watch what stops and what keeps working.

items: Switch airplane mode on and note the icon in the status bar.
Try to send a message and read the error, without worrying.
Open the camera and take a photo, which still works.
Turn the mode off and watch the signal bars return.
Send the same message and confirm it leaves.

body.text: You now know a switch that saves battery, data, and temper. In the next lesson you will free space on a phone that says its storage is full.

excerpt: What fills a phone's storage, which items are safe to delete, how to move photos off before you run out, and the settings that stop the pile growing back.

body.text: This lesson explains what to do when a phone says its storage is full. You will see where the space went, delete what is safe, and move photos somewhere you can keep them. Nothing on the phone needs to be wiped.
Storage is the space your phone keeps for photos, videos, apps, and messages. When that space is full, the phone cannot take a new picture or install an update, and it starts to slow down.
Before you start

items: The phone with the warning.
About thirty minutes, and a charger.
Somewhere to keep photos: a computer, a memory card, or a cloud account.

body.text: See what is taking the space

items: Open Settings, then Storage, or Device care on Samsung phones.
Read the list from largest to smallest.
Photos and videos are usually first on a phone used for family pictures.
Apps are usually second, and WhatsApp is often the largest of them.
Tap each category to see the items inside it.
Note the free space at the top before you change anything.

body.text: You will see a coloured bar at the top of the storage screen, with each category in its own colour. The number beside it, such as 4.2 GB free, is the one that matters.

body.alt: A phone storage settings screen showing categories and free space.
body.caption: The coloured bar shows where the space went. The free figure at the top is what the phone is complaining about.

body.text: It looks like the phone needs replacing. A phone that cannot save a photo has too much stored in it, and clearing space brings it back to normal speed.
Delete what is safe, in this order

items: Clear the cache first, which is temporary data and deletes nothing you made.
Delete videos you have already sent to family, since they are usually copies.
Remove apps you have not opened in three months, which frees a surprising amount.
Empty the trash or recently deleted folder, because deleted photos sit there for thirty days.
Delete downloaded films and music you no longer watch or play.
Leave system files and unknown folders alone, because the phone needs them.

body.text: None of these steps remove a contact or a chat. Cached data and old downloads rebuild themselves if you need them again.

body.alt: A phone settings screen showing the option to clear cached data.
body.caption: Clearing cache frees space without touching photos, chats, or contacts. It is the safest first step.

body.text: Move photos instead of deleting them
Family photos are the last thing to delete and the first thing to rescue. Move them off the phone before the phone forces you to.

items: Copy the photo folder to a computer with a cable, which costs nothing.
Or use a memory card, if the phone has a slot for one.
Or upload to a cloud account, which needs data but keeps them safe from loss.
Check three photos on the new location before deleting anything from the phone.
Delete from the phone only after the copy is confirmed.
Note the date of the last backup somewhere you will see it.

body.text: Do not worry about doing it all in one evening. Moving a month of photos at a time is enough to keep the phone working.
Stop the space filling again

items: In WhatsApp, open Settings, then Storage and data, and turn off automatic media download.
Set the camera to a smaller video size, which saves a great deal of space.
Empty the trash every month, on the same day as something you already remember.
Uninstall an app when you finish with it rather than leaving it idle.
Turn on automatic backup if your data allows it, so photos leave the phone on their own.
Check the storage figure once a month, which takes ten seconds.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here has a route back, and the first one is the most common.

items: You deleted a photo by mistake: check the trash or recently deleted album within thirty days.
WhatsApp says storage is full but the phone has space: clear the app cache in Settings.
The phone still runs slowly: storage was one cause, and too many background apps is another.
An update will not install: it needs about twice the download size free. Clear more.
Photos did not copy to the computer: check the cable and choose file transfer, not charging.
The memory card is not seen: reseat it, or format it in the phone before first use.

body.text: Practice
Ten minutes today saves an evening later.

items: Open the storage screen and write down the free space.
Clear the cache of the two largest apps.
Empty the trash folder.
Copy twenty photos to a computer and check three of them.
Read the free space again and compare.

body.text: You can now keep a phone working for years past the first warning. In the next lesson you will decide what an app may see when it asks for the camera or your location.

excerpt: Why apps ask to use the camera, microphone, contacts, or location, how to answer each request, and how to take a permission back later.

body.text: This lesson explains the permission requests your phone shows: camera, microphone, contacts, and location. You will learn why an app asks, when the answer should be yes, and how to take a permission back afterwards.
A permission is the phone asking your consent before an app uses something private. The app cannot open the camera or read your contacts until you agree.
Before you start

items: A phone with a few apps installed.
Five minutes.

body.text: Read the question properly

items: Read the whole sentence, which names the app and the thing it wants.
Look at the three buttons: allow, allow once, and don't allow.
Choose allow once when you are unsure and want to test the app.
Choose don't allow if the request makes no sense for that app.
The app usually still works, with that one feature switched off.
You can change your mind later in Settings, which is the point of the buttons.

body.text: You will see a small box in the middle of the screen with the app name at the top and the permission in a sentence below. The three buttons sit underneath, and nothing happens until you tap one.

body.alt: A phone screen showing an app permission request with allow and deny buttons.
body.caption: The box names the app and the permission. No answer means no access, so there is no rush.

body.text: It looks like refusing will break the app. Most apps work with the camera or location denied, and only the feature that needs it stops.
Which requests are reasonable
Match the request to what the app is for. A request that has no connection to the app's job deserves a refusal.

items: A camera app needs the camera, and that request is fair.
A maps app needs location while you are navigating.
A messaging app needs the microphone only when you record a voice note.
A torch app asking for your contacts is a warning sign.
A game asking for your location is rarely necessary.
A bank app may need the camera for a document check, and it should say why.

body.alt: A settings screen listing which apps may use the camera.
body.caption: Every permission can be reviewed in one place. You can close access to an app that no longer needs it.

body.text: Taking a permission back

items: Open Settings, then Apps, then the app you want to check.
Tap Permissions to see the list and the current answer for each.
Change camera, microphone, or location to don't allow.
On a phone that offers it, set location to while using the app rather than always.
Open Settings, then Privacy, to see a dashboard of what was used recently.
Check the list every few months, since apps you installed for one job often keep access.

body.text: None of this removes the app or its data. Changing a permission affects only what the app may use from now on.
Do not worry if you allowed something in a hurry. Every permission is one screen away from being closed again.
Location: the three choices
Location is the permission that matters most, and the phone gives you three answers rather than two.

items: Allow all the time suits almost nothing, except a tracking app you chose on purpose.
Allow while using the app is right for maps, ride apps, and delivery.
Don't allow still lets a map work if you type the address yourself.
The phone shows a small arrow in the status bar when location is in use.
Turn on precise location only when a driver needs to find you.
Switch location off completely from quick settings when you want nothing to know.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is reversible, and the phone tells you what changed.

items: The camera will not open in an app: the permission is denied. Allow it in Settings.
A voice note records silence: the microphone is denied for that app.
Maps show the wrong town: precise location is off, or location is denied.
A permission keeps appearing: the app asks again each time it needs the feature, which is normal after a refusal.
Photos will not send to contacts: the app lacks permission to read contacts, not photos.
An app stopped working after an update: a new version often asks for a new permission.

body.text: Practice
A five-minute review of one app is enough to understand the whole system.

items: Pick one app you use daily and open its permissions.
Read each permission and ask what the app needs it for.
Set location to while using the app.
Close any permission that makes no sense for that app.
Open the app and check that it still does its main job.

body.text: You can now answer a permission box with a reason instead of a guess. In the next lesson you will lock a phone and a laptop so nobody else can open them.
